There's a new PM title showing up in job postings: Forward Deployed Product Manager. Scale AI, BetterUp, and Accenture are just a few hiring for it. I read their job description to see what the role actually does.

Dr. Nancy Li called it "the new hot Product role" where a traditional PM asks, "What should we build?”. An FDPM asks, "How do we make this actually work for the customer and expand the account's value?"

Here's what one of the postings says about the job:

1. You own product outcomes for the highest-impact enterprise accounts. You're the PM accountable for delivery and the value the customer gets.
2. You take deployments from a signed contract into production. 
3. You turn real customer workflows, friction, and priorities into product input for the core platform teams. That input is specific, backed by evidence, and clear about tradeoffs.
4. You partner closely with forward deployed engineers (FDEs), so the account runs as one coordinated team.
5. You find room to expand the account, based on value the customer has already seen.

My read is that this is really a role for an experienced PM who owns delivery for one specific customer profile. You’re still on the hook for product outcomes, just for the highest-impact enterprise accounts. Your team works more like customer-facing engineers who get a working solution deployed, and the PM decides what to improve once it’s live. Along the way, you might also scope features that end up helping the broader platform and every type of customer. You’ll leverage data to improve and fine-tune what the customer will experience. 

I recommend PMs to double down on the soft skills they’ve built and start to apply a systems thinking mindset when asking to turn real workflows into production-level experiences. You’ll be able to transition to this type of role as more companies adopt LLMs/non-deterministic products to their offerings.

I think this is the best time there has ever been to start a business. I'm less convinced it's a good time to rely on someone else employing you.

A microagi campaign at Berlin airport recently got me thinking about this. It reminded me of Apple's "Think Different" ads. I looked into the company afterwards: physical AI, bringing robots into the real world.

Meanwhile, I watch AI get better at drafting legal documents, reviewing contracts and answering legal questions. Work that commands expensive human time is becoming something software can do.

Compare that with cleaning a toilet. A robot needs to handle the room, the objects and the unexpected. It needs hardware, installation and maintenance. The labour cost it replaces may be much lower.

Legal AI has costs too. But it doesn't need a machine installed in every bathroom.

That's why I expect a lot of desk-based work to come under pressure before many physical jobs do. Sitting at a computer is no longer the safe side of that divide.

My bet is that companies will need fewer people to produce the same output. Some jobs will change. Others won't be filled again. I don't expect new roles to neatly absorb everyone whose work disappears.

But the same economics change what I can build on my own.

A prototype, a website, sales material, finance workflows. I can take on work that would previously have required hiring people or paying outside specialists. I still need customers, judgment and a reason for the business to exist. I need less organisation around me to get started.

I expect more people to become self-employed. Some because they see the opportunity. Others because the job they expected is no longer there.

I'd rather start learning how to build and sell now than wait for an employer to decide how much of my work still needs me.

I'd appreciate a little help from my network.

I'm currently open to permanent remote opportunities and contract engagements.

I bring over 10 years of professional experience across IT and technology, with a career spanning hardware contracting, networking, IT support, frontend and backend software development, cloud and platform engineering, DevOps/DevSecOps, cybersecurity, and AI infrastructure.

One thing that has shaped my approach to technology is that I don't see these disciplines as isolated skills. I understand how they connect across the technology lifecycle — from building software and designing infrastructure to securing systems, deploying applications, and operating them reliably in production.

I'm particularly interested in opportunities where I can help companies solve complex technical challenges, build and scale technology products, strengthen their infrastructure, and bring AI solutions into production.

I'm also interested in Forward Deployed Engineering, working closely with customers and business teams to understand their challenges and translate them into practical, production-ready technical solutions.

I'm open to opportunities with startups and established companies, and would welcome conversations with founders, CTOs, engineering leaders, and hiring teams.

If you're hiring, know a company looking for someone with this background, or can introduce me to someone who might benefit from my experience, I'd genuinely appreciate a recommendation or introduction.

I'm open to exploring the right opportunity, whether permanent or contract-based.

Thank you to everyone willing to help or share this with someone in their network.

There’s a new sexy job everyone is hiring.

It’s not finance. It’s not consulting. It’s not even engineering.

It is the highly coveted Creator in Residence role! 

I read 20 of the job ads...and only 1 asked for a follower count.

I’m obviously talking about the creator in residence: the person a company hires to be its face and voice online. (In my case the title is Head of New Media at Sifted, same idea.)

No degree required. But you can’t really apply your way in either. You need receipts, and that means working almost 2 jobs for about 6 months.

People message me almost every day asking how to get one. 

So I did the homework. 20 roles, most from 2026: AI start-ups, a London VC, a kombucha brand and (my personal favourite) The Rock’s tequila company.

3 things surprised me:

1️⃣ Followers barely matter
19 of the 20 asked for a portfolio, a reel or proof you’d grown something. If you’ve been waiting for a magic number before you feel “allowed” to want this job, you can stop waiting.

2️⃣ The pay range is absurd

17 November 2023. This is me on the bridge of my last ship, one last time.
I usually never record my sign-offs. But I’d sailed with a captain who would take a moment to thank the bridge after a good contract. That day, I thought I’d do the same. I went around touching the equipment I’d worked with and recorded it.
My plan was clear. Sign off, get married, finish my Chief Mate courses, clear my exams and go back as a Chief Officer.
I finished both Chief mates Phase 1&2 , sat some of the exams. I thought I’d take a contractual job ashore while I studied for the rest. I’d spent years working towards the next rank, but I started asking myself what I could do if I put that same effort into a career ashore. If it didn’t work out, I could always go back to sea.
I applied for over 100 jobs in India and abroad. Two companies called me back.
The hardest part was explaining what I’d done at sea in a way that made sense to someone hiring ashore. Then I read the NAVTOR job description and thought, this is exactly the experience I have.
I took the job. Within four months, I was in Norway. That’s a story in itself.
Over the last two years, I’ve visited customers and talked through problems I recognised from my own time onboard. It made it easier to understand where they were coming from, and I realised how much of my experience at sea I was still using every day.
When I was sailing, I used to see photos of shipping events and wonder what happened in those rooms. This past year, I attended the World Maritime Forum in Copenhagen. Last week, I presented to a room full of customers and sat on a panel in Hamburg. Seeing those photos afterwards felt pretty surreal.
Along the way, I got to do an MBA at SP Jain School of Global Management - Dubai, Mumbai, Singapore & Sydney. I have one final presentation left. I also started a podcast and spoke to around 12 people about how they moved ashore. Around this time last year, I posted a video about my own story. It got around 50,000 views, and the page is now close to 25,000 followers. The part I enjoy most is when a seafarer reaches out and I can help them think through what they want to do next.
To everyone at NAVTOR who gave me a chance, answered my questions when I was new ashore and trusted me to take on more, thank you. A lot of people helped me along the way. I remember what you did for me.
I’m now moving into an AI Transformation role at NAVTOR. There’s a lot to learn again, and I’m looking forward to it. When I recorded that clip on the bridge, I had no idea where any of this would go.

531 AI film job postings reveal what studios actually want to hire: not operators, but authors.

JP Holecka, founder of POWER SHIFTER Digital, analyzed over 500 job postings from 2024 to 2026 to understand what's changing in AI film hiring. The data shows a dramatic shift. Generic "AI Artist" roles fell from 36% of postings in 2025 to 25% in 2026, while filmmaker and director roles more than doubled to 16%. Employers are now using film-grammar vocabulary like shot, framing and coverage in 41% of listings, up from 17% a year ago, according to LBB Online.

What employers keep paying for is consistency: character and visual continuity across sequences, named in 35% of postings year over year. That discipline separates a production team from a talented person working alone. Most of this work is bought by the project (51% contract), with salaried roles clustering around $120K median.

If you're building an AI film career, the market is moving away from tool expertise toward storytelling and visual authorship. Studios want someone who can hold a vision steady across a production and answer for the final cut. If you're hiring, the data suggests you should ask for a reel and how they maintain consistency, not what software they use.

Build your free AICS profile to showcase the work that matters: your reel, your visual consistency, your storytelling.

Why 'Offshore Talent Is Lower Quality' Is the Most Expensive Myth in Tech Hiring

Seventy three percent of UK employers say they cannot fill the roles they have.
And a surprising number of them still describe offshore talent as lower quality.
That figure comes from ManpowerGroup's 2026 Talent Shortage Survey, against seventy two percent globally. Software engineering is one of the hardest areas to recruit for, and AI skills are now the single hardest skill to find.
So here is my argument. The belief that offshore talent is lower quality is the most expensive myth in tech hiring, and it is expensive in a very specific way. It keeps a senior role open for months while the roadmap slips.
Look at what the people who actually buy this are doing. Deloitte's global outsourcing research found that eighty percent of executives plan to maintain or increase their investment in third party outsourcing. These are not people guessing.
Does that mean offshore never goes wrong? Of course not, and I would be lying if I said otherwise. Some engagements fail. The cause is usually one of a few things.
A vague brief. No real technical assessment. Contracts that say nothing clear about who owns the code. No paid trial before a long commitment.
None of those are geography problems. They are process problems, and they would sink a UK permanent hire just as easily. A confident interview does not tell you whether someone can ship.
The same discipline applies to the work itself. Ask to see real code. Run a scoped task in your own stack. Speak to people who have worked with the engineer before. Those steps catch weak candidates in London and Lagos alike, and they are the steps a rushed process skips first.
Quality is a property of the vetting, not of the postcode. The strongest engineers in the world are not distributed according to where your office happens to be.
Compliance concerns are real, too, and I would never wave them away. But right to work, IP assignment and employment structure are reasons to ask any provider for its position in writing, not reasons to rule the model out.
So the question for a CIO is not whether offshore quality is lower.
It is whether your own hiring process, onshore or offshore, would survive being measured as honestly as you measure a vendor.
When did you last test yours?

Are you hiring for a programme in the GCC next year? 

A few early decisions will save you months later.

If you hire only strategists, you might find that nobody can build the plan, nobody knows the regulators, and the contract won't let you swap out a weak hire.

Here are 5 things to check before you start.

  • Builders next to strategists. 
A plan is only useful if someone can build it: the product, the data, the systems.

If you bring builders in late, they spend weeks catching up on a plan they didn't shape. 

Put them on the team from day one.

  • Local depth. 
Make sure your hires know local rules and regulations; if they have to get up to speed on this, you've already lost time.

  • Easy to exit. 
Long contracts are hard to undo if the wrong person turns up.

Split the work into stages and ask suppliers for free swaps, so changing course costs little.

  • Handover in the plan. 
When the experts leave, someone has to run and maintain what they built. 

Make time for your own people to learn the work while the experts are still there.

  • AI checks. 
AI can hallucinate and so ask every supplier how they check claims before a CV reaches you.

Which role can't your programme fill?

Using AI to write smart contracts? Treat the output as untrusted until it passes your own gates.

Two recent studies, a 2025 workshop paper from the University of Genoa and a 2026 preprint from Deakin University, found that AI-generated Solidity can compile and look complete while still carrying serious security flaws. Both conclude it needs human-led checks before deployment.

Five gates to run before an external audit:
1. Write the spec (what must always be true) before the prompt
2. Compile cleanly and run static analysis on every pull request
3. Test beyond the happy path: fuzz and invariant tests
4. Review line by line, and mark which parts were AI-generated
5. Hand auditors the spec, tests and triaged findings

Law and accounting are often named as the careers most at risk from AI. In one room in the South West, those were the firms still planning to hire juniors.

Taught by Humans and techSPARK uk brought together seven professional services firms as part of their AI Talent Pipeline South West research. Laura Gemmell's write-up found:

• All of them use AI across the whole firm, from Microsoft Copilot to legal tools such as Harvey and Legora.
• All of them plan to hire juniors in the next 12 months.
• Juniors and trainees are often the keenest users. Some longer-serving staff are more cautious.
• New roles are appearing: legal engineer, innovation paralegal, legal technologist. One legal engineer said her role didn't exist six months ago.

Seven firms is one room, not a survey. So we looked at the wider UK numbers:

• Law: training contracts at 109 leading law firms are down 1.7% for 2027, from 2,593 to 2,549. Legal Cheek, which tracks them, links most of the dip to firms taking on more solicitor apprentices.
• AI in law: 61% of UK lawyers were using generative AI at work in 2025, up from 46% in January that year. Just over half of them chose tools built for law.
• Accountancy: 68% of mid-tier firms expect AI to reduce demand for some early-career accountants, but 83% say that won't directly mean fewer roles overall. They expect graduate hiring to fall 40% and school-leaver hiring to rise 49%.
• AI in accountancy: 86% of those firms say their tech strategy explicitly includes AI.

So the junior roles are still there, but the way in is changing, and more of it runs through apprenticeships and school-leaver schemes. Laura makes a point students should hear too: young people are told law and accounting are most at risk, so some rule them out before they even apply.

Our take: if using AI well is now part of starting out, the question for a graduate is how to show it. "Confident with AI" is easy to write on a CV. But student-built project an employer can open, read and watch shows how you actually work, which is exactly what we're trying to Showcase.

AI attracts the capital. Can insurtechs prove their value?

AI-focused businesses received 99.1% of insurtech funding in Q2 2026 and 83.2% in Q3, according to Gallagher Re.

That concentration makes AI impossible to ignore. It also raises an important question for founders: how will your business stand out among companies making similar claims?

An insurance buyer needs to understand what changes after adopting your product.

Will their team make better decisions? Can they process more business? How difficult will implementation be? What will the product deliver that they cannot achieve through their existing technology or internal team?

Gallagher Re highlights this challenge as insurers and brokers develop their own AI capabilities.

For insurtechs, our view is that differentiation needs to run through the whole business.

Product teams need a detailed understanding of the customer’s workflow. Commercial teams need to explain value in terms the buyer can assess. Implementation teams need to deliver that value within the realities of an insurance organisation.

A gap between any of those functions can weaken an otherwise promising proposition.

This has direct implications for hiring.

Technical capability is essential. So is the ability to connect it to insurance problems, navigate customer organisations and support adoption after the contract is signed.

For some businesses, the missing hire may be a product leader with strong insurance knowledge. For others, it may be someone who can bring discipline to implementation or build a more repeatable commercial process.

The right answer depends on where customer value is getting lost.

At FinPro., we believe that is a useful starting point for any growth conversation: identify the gap between what the technology can do and what the customer actually experiences.

Then build the team to close it.

Where is the hardest part of proving AI’s value today: the product, the business case or implementation?

Next: what this looks like in established insurance markets.

The skills AI can't automate are now the hardest to hire for.
 
AI tools now write boilerplate code, draft test cases, summarise tickets and generate documentation in minutes. Routine, well-defined work is getting faster and cheaper.
 
What has not become easier is hiring for the work around it. The skills that remain human are the ones that are hardest to see on a resume, hardest to test in an interview and slowest to build.
 
Here are 6 of them, and why they are tough to hire for.
 
1. Problem framing
 The skill: turning a vague business need into a clear, solvable problem before a single line of code is written.
 The hiring challenge: it rarely appears as a keyword. It shows only when a candidate asks the right questions.
 
2. System design and architectural judgement
 The skill: making trade-offs between scalability, cost, security and maintainability.
 The hiring challenge: tools can generate a design, but only experience can say whether it will hold at scale.
 
3. Critical review of AI output
 The skill: spotting the subtle bug, the hallucinated function or the security gap in generated code and content.
 The hiring challenge: it needs depth in the fundamentals, so junior profiles with tool fluency alone often cannot do it.
 
4. Stakeholder communication
 The skill: translating technical risk into business language, and managing expectations with product, clients and leadership.
 The hiring challenge: it is judged by how someone talks, not by what is listed in the skills section.
 
5. Ownership and accountability
 The skill: taking responsibility for outcomes in production, not just for the ticket assigned.
 The hiring challenge: it only becomes visible under pressure, long after the offer is accepted.
 
6. Learning agility
 The skill: picking up a new tool, domain or framework quickly and applying it with judgement.
 The hiring challenge: certificates show what someone studied, not how fast they adapt.
 
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR HIRING
 The situation many teams face: the job description lists ten tools, but the real need is judgement, ownership and communication. Interviews test syntax while projects fail on ambiguity.
 
What works better:
 - Scenario-based and work-sample assessments over trivia rounds
 - Structured behavioural interviews with a clear scorecard
 - Skills-based hiring that looks at demonstrated capability, not only job titles
 - Contract or contract-to-hire engagements to evaluate fit on real work
 - A talent pool built around these skills before the requirement becomes urgent

 AI is raising the baseline for tools. It is raising the premium for judgement. The most valuable hire is no longer the person who knows the most tools, but the one who knows what to do when the tool is wrong.

Your mindset is very, very important. But what you feed your mind is just as important.

Yesterday, I posted about the importance of being careful about what we feed our minds and the kind of things we listen to.

I also talked about how easy it is to start believing that something isn’t working simply because that’s all you keep hearing or reading about it.

And guess what? I got another contract offer on Upwork yesterday. 

It got me thinking about something.

Imagine constantly hearing things like Upwork is dead, Fiverr is dead, nobody is hiring, there is no money in this industry, and so on.

If that’s all you keep hearing, at some point, you’ll start believing it. You’ll even begin to approach opportunities with that same mindset.

But the truth is, people are still getting jobs on Upwork. People are still making money on Fiverr. People are getting clients through LinkedIn and other platforms.

Yes, things might be challenging, and getting clients might not be as easy as it used to be, but that doesn’t mean the opportunities are no longer there.

Sometimes, we need to stop focusing so much on what isn’t working for other people and start looking at what is working for those who are getting results.

Be careful what you feed your mind. It matters more than you think.

And please, don’t let someone else’s experience convince you that you can’t get the results you’re looking for.

We keep going! 🚀
